title: Fraud Detection Enterprise Pilot Playbook and Technical FAQ
author: Liam Chen
body:
Overview:

Purpose: This playbook equips sales, solutions engineering, and customer success teams to run a high-velocity enterprise pilot for fraud detection/transaction-monitoring workloads using Redwood Inference. It consolidates positioning, competitive points, pilot architecture options (hosted, dedicated, private), pricing guidance, runbook-style rollout steps, target success metrics, a customer case study, and a prospect-focused Security FAQ.

Audience: Platform/infra engineers, fraud ops managers, ML engineers, CTO/CISO stakeholders at prospective financial services, payments, and fintech customers.

Executive summary:
- Problem: Real-time and near-real-time fraud detection requires predictable latency (<= 50ms P95 for scoring), high throughput for peak windows (thousands TPS), and strong auditability and data controls for regulated environments.
- Redwood value prop for fraud use cases:
  - Low-latency inference primitives with KV cache and continuous batching to meet P95 latency SLOs.
  - Flexible deployment: quick hosted API pilot, predictable Dedicated pools for throughput, Private (VPC/on‑prem) for regulated data.
  - Cost-performance controls: batching, cache, and quantization recommendations tuned to transaction length distributions.
  - Observability and rollback: token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-model tracing, automatic fallback to cheaper model variants.

Messaging by persona (short scripts):
- CTO: "Move from experimentation to production without rebuilding inference plumbing — Redwood gives predictable latency, autoscaling GPU pools, and enterprise controls so your fraud detection models can run at scale with predictable economics."
- CISO: "We support private control planes, KMS integrations, audit logs, and retrospective model scoring traces; you control keys and retention policies."
- Fraud Ops / Head of Risk: "Enable canary scoring and A/B rollback by user segment; monitor precision/recall drift per rule and tie alerts to the Redwood Console."
- ML Engineer: "Ship models with the same API across environments, pin model versions for rollouts, and use built-in quantization and batching suggestions to reduce inference cost without retraining."

Competitive brief (quick hit):
- Major cloud managed endpoints (AWS Sagemaker Endpoints, GCP Vertex AI): strong infra history but often slower per-token for autoregressive LLM scoring at scale and limited integrated prefix caching and model-fallback policies. Redwood: engineered for inference economics (batching/cache/quantization) and simpler multi-environment parity.
- LLM API vendors: easier for prototyping but limited on-prem/private deployment and enterprise-grade throughput commitments. Redwood: hosted for speed, Dedicated for committed throughput, Private for regulated deployments.
- Specialized scoring vendors (traditional fraud SaaS): highly tuned rules engines but lack generative-model contextualization and LLM-based enrichment for novel fraud patterns. Redwood pairs with your rules and enrichers, not a replacement for domain rules.

Pilot sizing and architecture options:
1) Hosted Quickstart (2–4 weeks) — best for early signal on model accuracy and false positive reduction
   - Components: Redwood hosted API + customer-supplied anonymized historical sample (or synthetic), evaluation harness in customer staging, Redwood Console access for tracing.
   - Typical config: 10 TPS sustained, burst 200 TPS; model: small LLM embedder + reranker; expected latency: P95 40–120ms depending on model.
   - Deliverables: baseline false-positive rate (FPR), true-positive rate (TPR), latency report, cost-per-1M requests estimate.

2) Dedicated Pilot (6–12 weeks) — for predictable throughput and economics
   - Components: Reserved GPU pool (Redwood Dedicated), canary traffic routing, can integrate with customer VPC peering, SSO for ops.
   - Typical config: 250–1,000 TPS sustained across GPUs; autoscale policy and burst buffer.
   - Deliverables: SLA targets (uptime 99.9%, P95 latency target), cost model for committed capacity, integration checklist for rollout.

3) Private / On‑prem (8–16 weeks) — for regulated customers
   - Components: Customer-managed VPC or air-gapped on‑prem package, KMS/HSM integration, audit log export, signed attestation.
   - Deliverables: security evidence pack, SCG/PRD for SOC2/PCI readiness, runbook for upgrades and rollback.

Pilot success criteria (sample measurable metrics):
- Accuracy: Delta TPR >= +6% and Delta FPR <= -15% vs existing baseline on labeled holdout (or equivalent business metric reduction: false positive reduction -> lower manual review costs).
- Latency: End-to-end scoring P95 <= 50ms (hosted) or configured SLO met on Dedicated/Private.
- Throughput: Sustain peak TPS for 10 minute windows per customer peak profile.
- Economics: Cost per 1M transactions <= customer target (example calc below) and unit cost improvement vs current vendor.
- Observability: Model drift alerts configured; per-route dashboards created in Redwood Console.

Pricing guidance and worked example:
- Pricing levers: per-token (hosted), committed GPU capacity (Dedicated), private license + support (Private). Add-ons: extended observability retention, SOC2 evidence pack.
- Example Hosted pilot cost estimate (illustrative):
  - Assumptions: average scoring request 120 tokens (embedding + brief context), 1M requests over pilot window.
  - Calculation: 1M requests * 120 tokens = 120M tokens. Hosted rate (example) $0.0006 per token -> $72,000.
  - Optimizations: prefix caching and batching can reduce tokens consumed by ~20–40% on typical enrichment flows -> adjusted cost $43k–$58k.

- Example Dedicated pricing approach (illustrative):
  - Reserved pool sized for 500 TPS sustained -> monthly commit $XXk (custom quoting). Typical pilot commitment: 1–3 months. Dedicated often yields 30–60% lower unit cost at scale.

- Negotiation tips:
  - Frame hosted pilot as discovery and commit to scale if cost targets met.
  - Offer credits for integration work or extended console retention in pilot phase.
  - Use cost-savings estimates from batching/quantization to justify committed capacity.

Rollout and runbook (6-phase compressed):
1) Discovery (Week 0–1): define success metrics, get sample data, agree compliance requirements and NDA scoping. Owner: SE + Customer Fraud Lead.
2) Staging integration (Week 1–2): ingest sample events, configure evaluation harness, Redwood Console access. Deliver baseline reports.
3) Model validation (Week 2–3): run labeled holdout tests and A/B scoring, produce precision/recall and user-story impact.
4) Canary (Week 3–5): 1–5% live traffic routing, monitor latency, drift, manual-review reduction.
5) Ramp (Week 5–8): expand traffic with planned rollback gates; SRE verifies autoscaling and Dedicated capacity.
6) Production handoff (Week 8+): transition to customer ops, set recurring health reviews and QBR cadence.

Security & compliance FAQ (prospect-facing):
Q: Is customer data sent to Redwood in hosted pilots?
A: For hosted pilots we recommend anonymized or synthetic samples whenever possible. When production sample data is required, we support encrypted transfers, tenant isolation, and contractual data handling controls. For regulated customers we push Private or Dedicated deployments.

Q: Can you integrate with our KMS/HSM?
A: Yes. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations. For Dedicated we support KMS integrations depending on contract scope.

Q: How long are logs and traces retained?
A: Default retention in piloted hosted tiers is 30 days. Options for extended retention (90 days, 1 year) are available as an add-on. All retention policies are configurable per-customer.

Q: Do you provide evidence for audits (SOC2/PCI)?
A: We provide a security evidence pack for pilot customers (redacted) and can coordinate SOC2 or PCI attestation support during Private deployments.

Q: What isolation model do you provide for Dedicated?
A: Dedicated provides isolated GPU pools, configurable VPC/network isolation, and per-tenant encryption at rest.

Q: Can model outputs be fully logged for explainability?
A: Yes — Redwood Console can persist model inputs, outputs, and traces for audit. Logging levels and PII redaction policies are configurable.

Prospect objection handling (short bullets):
- "We can’t trust managed providers with PII": Offer Private or Dedicated, show KMS/HSM and audit log options, provide remediation checklist.
- "Latency is too variable": Surface P95 numbers from bench and recommend Dedicated with autoscale and caching.
- "Cost is unpredictable": Show cost modeling with batching and quantization levers and offer committed pool pricing.

Case study (anonymized bank; example results):
- Customer profile: Global payments processor, ~1.2B transactions/year, existing rule-based stack with heavy manual review load.
- Pilot objective: Reduce manual review volume while maintaining or improving fraud capture rate.
- Pilot scope: 120k historical labeled events + 3 day live canary; Hosted pilot -> Dedicated commit after positive signal.
- Outcomes after 3 months:
  - Manual review workload reduced by 38%.
  - False positives reduced 18% on holdout.
  - Average scoring P95 latency 42ms (hosted) -> moved to Dedicated with 99.9% uptime SLA.
  - Unit inference cost reduced 44% after moving to Dedicated and enabling KV caching.
- Key lessons learned: anonymize samples early, define rollback gates per segment, instrument drift metrics tied to business ops.

Appendix: YAML example for canary routing policy (example)
```yaml
canary_policy:
  route_percentage: 5
  monitor_metrics:
    - latency_p95_threshold_ms: 100
    - manual_review_rate_threshold_pct: 10
  rollback_on:
    - latency_p95_exceed: true
    - false_positive_increase_pct: 10
```

2) Request anonymized 30k event sample and business labels.
3) Provision hosted sandbox and unit tests in 48–72 hours.
4) Run baseline evaluation, produce one-slide results and recommended pilot configuration.
5) If economics look favorable, propose Dedicated sizing and commit timeline.
